A standalone CMake project is included so the target relationships can be inspected without the series’ larger build surrounding them.

topics.title: 2.1.1 Creating Executable Targets
topics.summary: An executable target names its source files and the libraries it consumes. CMake’s configure step constructs the build graph; the build step invokes the selected compiler and linker. A successful configure does not prove the program compiles, and a successful build does not prove its runtime behavior.

topics.title: 2.1.2 Creating Library Targets
topics.summary: A library target gives related implementation files a reusable build identity. STATIC creates an archive for later linking; SHARED creates a dynamically linked library; INTERFACE can carry header-only usage requirements without producing an ordinary compiled library artifact.

blocks.text: Target names are logical build names, not necessarily installed filenames. Prefer linking the logical target to typing a guessed archive path. That lets CMake order prerequisites, propagate requirements, and account for platform-specific naming. A target still needs a deliberate install/export policy before it becomes a consumable package.

topics.title: Defining Independent Library and Executable Targets in CMake
topics.summary: Target-based CMake models actual build products and lets each product carry the requirements consumers need.

blocks.text: Defining Independent Library and Executable Targets in CMake
rich: Defining Independent Library and Executable Targets in CMake
blocks.headingContext: Defining Independent Library and Executable Targets in CMake

blocks.text: Purpose
rich: Purpose

blocks.text: Target-based CMake models actual build products and lets each product carry the requirements consumers need.
rich: Target-based CMake models actual build products and lets each product carry the requirements consumers need.

blocks.text: Code or command
rich: Code or command

blocks.text:
add_library(mathlib src/add.cpp)
target_include_directories(mathlib PUBLIC include)
target_compile_features(mathlib PUBLIC cxx_std_20)

add_executable(calculator app/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(calculator PRIVATE mathlib)
blocks.code:
add_library(mathlib src/add.cpp)
target_include_directories(mathlib PUBLIC include)
target_compile_features(mathlib PUBLIC cxx_std_20)

add_executable(calculator app/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(calculator PRIVATE mathlib)

blocks.text: What the important parts do
rich: What the important parts do

blocks.text: `add_library` and `add_executable` create two distinct nodes in the build graph. The library publishes its include directory and C++ standard requirement; the executable links to the library instead of inheriting unrelated global flags.
rich: `add_library` and `add_executable` create two distinct nodes in the build graph. The library publishes its include directory and C++ standard requirement; the executable links to the library instead of inheriting unrelated global flags.

blocks.text: CMake generates build rules in which `mathlib` is built before `calculator` when needed.

topics.title: 2.2.1 Propagating Include Directories
topics.summary: An include directory is PUBLIC when the target and its consumers need it, PRIVATE when only the implementation needs it, and INTERFACE when only consumers need the requirement. Public headers that include other public headers must have their search requirements available to consumers.

topics.title: 2.2.2 Propagating Compile Definitions and Options
topics.summary: Compile features express a language requirement such as cxx_std_20. Definitions should propagate only when consumers must see the same interface-relevant setting. An implementation’s warning preferences are normally private; a macro changing a public class layout is an ABI concern that cannot safely vary between producer and consumer.

rich: Propagating PUBLIC and PRIVATE Target Requirements

blocks.text: Purpose

blocks.text: The point of target dependencies is not just link order; usage requirements must propagate only when consumers actually need them.
rich: The point of target dependencies is not just link order; usage requirements must propagate only when consumers actually need them.

blocks.text: Code or command
rich: Code or command

blocks.text:
add_library(core src/core.cpp)
target_include_directories(core PUBLIC include PRIVATE src)
target_compile_definitions(core PRIVATE CORE_BUILD=1)

add_executable(app app/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE core)
blocks.code:

target_include_directories(core PUBLIC include PRIVATE src)
target_compile_definitions(core PRIVATE CORE_BUILD=1)

add_executable(app app/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE core)

blocks.text: What the important parts do
rich: What the important parts do

blocks.text: `PUBLIC include` is visible both while building `core` and while compiling consumers. `PRIVATE src` and `CORE_BUILD=1` affect only the library implementation. `app` gets the public interface requirements by linking the target.
